- A platform block is a boundary, not an obstacle.
- The platform's policy is a validated resource, so the Planner plans only inside it.
- On a block the Checker gives HALT, the Reflector records the policy and a permitted path, and the Orchestrator returns ESCALATE or INTERRUPT.
- Trail products name their permitted path and ship their boundary constraints, because the buyer becomes bound by the platform's terms.
- The rule holds on Grok Bot, Claude computer use and your own runtime.

**Maker → Checker.** These are the results from the real commands.
- **Build:** `build.ps1` regenerated 15 bots and 9 rules, and EC-0002 shows up in `AGENTS.md` and the Chief files.
- **Checks:** the queue check passes over 2 items, the layout check passes, and `dotnet test` passes 6 of 6.
- **Commit:** I made the local commit `62adf4e`, which did not push.

**Validation results.** Two of these change your setup.
- **Grok Bot limits:** an account can have up to 50 Bots and group chats combined, so 15 bots plus the Round Tables fit. A group chat holds two to six Bots, which matches the 6-member Executive Round Table you already have.
- **Shared computer:** files and sign-ins on the shared computer aren't isolated per Bot. The Cursor team docs advise that when a workload needs its own computer and credential set, give it its own Cursor user. So a Chief's Checker only gets real isolation on a separate Cursor user, not on a separate Bot.
- **CFO ceiling:** there is no Grok Bot-specific spend cap; the on-demand control on your Cursor account is the only ceiling. That is where your CFO dollar figure has to be set.
- **Routine cost:** routines spend usage every time they run, and an hourly schedule or a busy Slack listener can use a week of usage in a day. Prefer event triggers to schedules.
- **MAF Agent Skills (.NET):** it has left experimental preview and the API is stable, with human-in-the-loop approval among the production controls. That supports your reject/approve gate on skill calls.
- **Versions:** the latest .NET release I found is dotnet-1.12.0, released 2 Jul. Your `Directory.Packages.props` pins Microsoft.Agents.AI 1.23.0, which is higher than that tag, so I couldn't confirm 1.23.0 from that page. Hosting and DevUI are marked preview and the OpenAI hosting package is alpha, so I'd keep those out of anything you sell.
- **Agent Governance Toolkit:** v3.7.0 (2026-05-18) is a Microsoft-signed public preview, production-quality but may have breaking changes before GA. It integrates with MAF through the middleware pipeline. Adopting it is an install, so it needs your go.

**Checker → Reflector.** I checked the search results against your repo's pins. I issue no verdict on either trail. A fresh Checker still has to review loop 2 of trail 0001 and trail 0002.

**Reflector.** EC-0002 was promoted on your approval of a policy, but RR-001 says promotion normally needs a check proven able to fail. A must-fail check for the boundary rule is still owed. Also, you never told me the candidate names for renaming "Checker", so I left the law alone.

  3. A mythic display layer, for example Athena for the Planner and Argus for the Checker, with the law text unchanged.

**I am the Chief of Staff, and I orchestrate your question by answering it and declining to write `05-check` from this session.**

**Your question.** Yes, the Maker's output can be chained straight into a check. The term you're after is the "augmented LLM": a model with tools, retrieval and memory. In Anthropic's "Building effective agents" write-up, your Maker is that building block, and the chain into a checker is what they call prompt chaining, with a gate between steps. The looped version, one model generating and another evaluating, is the evaluator-optimizer workflow. That's the same shape as Maker, Checker and Reflector.

**Why it still has to be a fresh session.** The chain only gives you a real check if the evaluator doesn't share the generator's context. This session wrote the boundary check and the proof for trail 0003, so it carries the same blind spots.

Trail 0003 shows it. The proof passed every sample its author wrote. Then four adversarial samples I wrote in a second pass all slipped through, and a fifth still does. A same-context check would have repeated the first result. So the Checker stays a fresh, read-only session that re-runs the proof itself and writes its own samples. I won't write `05-check` or a PASS, LOOP or HALT here, because EC-004 says nobody scores their own work.

**The fastest way to run it properly.**
1. Open a new Claude Code session in the repo, with no history.
2. Paste the seed below.
3. It should write only `05-check.jsonl`, with exactly one verdict.

I could start that headless process from here, but it spends usage and you deferred that earlier, so tell me "run it" if you want me to. A headless run would still be a separate process with no Maker context.

**Checker → Reflector.** I checked nothing new this turn. I gave you an answer to the pattern question.

**Reflector.** The lesson is that "the chain can check it" and "the Maker can check it" are different claims. The chain can, but only across a context boundary. That fits what you had in mind for each Chief: a team whose members embody plan, make and check, with the check seat isolated from the make seat.
